Universal quotient/family flatness is over P and does not assert `P→S` flat.

([Stacks](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/download/artin.pdf), Lemma 98.12.3, pp. 18–19; Section 98.3, pp. 4–5).

The API gives `ParameterFormalExports.classify`: For a supplied θ and test T, its component gives `Hom_S(T,P)≃F(T)`; `ParameterFormalExports.universal`: The universal element is the image of `id_P`; `ParameterFormalExports.classify_natural`: Classifying `f∘g` agrees with pullback of classify(f) along g; `projectiveParameter_formalEquiv`: A quotient line of E at p has the deformation functor represented by `Ô_(P(E)),p`, under the quotient convention of §1.1; `grassmannParameter_formalEquiv`: Rank-r locally free quotient deformations are represented by the completed stalk of the supplied Grassmannian; `flagParameter_formalEquiv`: Compatible quotient flags at p have the completed-stalk formal universal property of the supplied flag scheme; `hilbertParameter_formalEquiv`: Deformations of the specified flat closed subscheme with fixed Hilbert polynomial are classified by the supplied Hilbert completion, with universal family pulled back; `quotParameter_formalEquiv`: Deformations of the specified flat quotient of E, modulo compatible quotient isomorphism, are classified by the supplied Quot completion; `homParameter_formalEquiv`: Deformations of a specified morphism in the supplied representable Hom functor are classified by its completed parameter stalk; `isomParameter_formalEquiv`: Deformations of a specified isomorphism are classified by the supplied Isom completion and retain the invertibility requirement.

*Needs:* `schemeFramedCompletionEquiv`, `spaceFramedEtaleCompletionEquiv`, Mathlib `CategoryTheory.yoneda`, Layers 1–2, SchemeAndStackFoundations Layer 1.

**Checks.**

- `ParameterTests.identityRepresentation`: For `F=Hom(-,P)` and θ=id, classify is the identity on actual arrows.
- `ParameterTests.universalElement`: The universal element classifies `id_P`, rather than a selected unrelated object.
- `ParameterTests.pullback`: Classifying a composition agrees with applying the contravariant functor map to the class of the outer arrow.
- `ParameterTests.grassmannEndpoints`: For E of rank n, rank-zero and rank-n quotient functors are terminal over S; over a rational field-base point their framed tangent is zero.
- `ParameterTests.hilbertNonflatBase`: For `S=Spec k[ε]` and `X=Spec k` closed in S, the degree-one Hilbert parameter is X. Its universal family over itself is flat although `X→S` is not flat; only Artinian S-maps satisfying `ε=0` are classified.
- `ParameterTests.quotLengthOne`: For `E=O` on `P¹_k`, a length-one quotient at a rational origin has point-deformation completion `k[[t]]`, since it is the length-one Hilbert functor of `P¹`.
- `ParameterTests.isomUnit`: For endomorphisms of the trivial line over A, Hom gives A and Isom gives A×; an Artinian endomorphism reducing to 1 is invertible, while zero is excluded.

Prove `arithmeticFormalComparison_transfer`. Given a supplied algebraic moduli stack M of the required elliptic/abelian objects, an equivalence between its framed fibre and the arithmetic deformation groupoid transports the completed-atlas presentation, infinitesimal stabilizers, tangent comparison and complete-local effectivity to that problem. If the formal object is effective and versal, the G-ring and limit-preservation inputs give a finite-type versal family via `effectiveVersal_algebraization`. A rigidifying level yields a represented local functor only after the supplied level theorem removes the required automorphisms. Coarse moduli alone does not supply this equivalence.

Here the arithmetic definition, the deformation theory and the algebraicity of the elliptic and abelian moduli stacks are hypotheses; no abelian or elliptic deformation theorem is proved here; for an Artin proof use `artin_stack_criterion` (§7.1) with each of its hypotheses verified; effectivity must be independently proved, for example by Grothendieck's existence theorem (SchemeAndStackFoundations §4.10) in its proper setting; For coherent families on an already fixed proper scheme use Grothendieck's existence theorem (SchemeAndStackFoundations §4.10); arbitrary varying formal schemes need a separate effectivity/algebraization theorem.

([Stacks](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/download/artin.pdf), Lemma 98.9.5, pp. 12–14; Lemma 98.12.7, pp. 20–21; Proposition 98.16.1 and Lemma 98.17.1, pp. 26–27).

For the proof, pull each general comparison through the supplied equivalence of framed groupoids, including arrows and universal objects; then for already algebraic M apply complete-local restriction; for a candidate category fibred in groupoids prove effectivity separately before applying `artin_stack_criterion`; then apply the effective-versal theorem with all hypotheses checked. Use only the precise automorphism-rigidity and parameter interfaces supplied for the chosen level.

*Needs:* `completedAtlasPresentation_equivalence`, `algebraicStackRestriction_equivalence`, `effectiveVersal_algebraization`, `ParameterFormalExports`, Layer 5, SchemeAndStackFoundations §4.10, `artin_stack_criterion`, `artin_space_criterion`, ModularCurves §7B, ModularCurves §7D.

### Examples

At the origin of the fixed node `xy=0`, a point has completed local ring `k[[x,y]]/(xy)` and tangent dimension two. Deforming the nodal curve is a different functor, with smoothing parameter t in `xy=t`. The framed automorphism group at BG is `ker(G(A)→G(k))`; at `A=k` this kernel is trivial. A padded chart `A¹`→point is versal and has a one-dimensional tangent kernel, so it is not a hull. For `[A¹/C₂]`, the coarse dual-number point `t=ε` has no square-root stack lift when 2 is invertible.

### Dependencies

Layers 6 and 7; SchemeAndStackFoundations §§4.2–4.4 (Artinian coefficient category, deformation functors, Schlessinger's theorem), §4.7 (formal schemes), §1.19 (representable diagonals) and §1.18 (2-fibre products).

## Layer 9: resolution and SNC compactification

The resolution input is supplied by
[ResolutionOfSingularitiesCharacteristicZero](../ResolutionOfSingularitiesCharacteristicZero/README.md).
The names in §§9.1–9.7 are consumption comparisons: they identify the named supplier exports with
the scheme, ideal-sheaf, blowup and SNC conventions used here. They retain the supplier's hypotheses
and naturality, including centre ideals and ordered boundary labels. The marked-ideal, Samuel and
invariant constructions and their finite-sequence existence theorems belong to that supplier.
The applications constructed here are the algebraic vanishing and numerical boundedness of
§§9.10–9.11. The comparisons also fix the interfaces for the rigidification and formal-moduli
carriers of Layers 5 and 8 without imposing smoothness on an arbitrary moduli stack.

### 9.1 Marked ideals, transforms and test equivalence

Use ResolutionOfSingularitiesCharacteristicZero Layer 1 on smooth finite-type schemes over any
characteristic-zero field. Its birth-ordered boundary enriches SchemeAndStackFoundations §4.17's
SNC data; forgetting birth order retains exactly that SNC divisor and its component labels.
Each comparison below uses the supplier export of the same name at the indicated section.

| Comparison names | Supplier section | Identified data and hypotheses |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `regularCoordinates` | §1.1 | Étale coordinates at closed points, completion over the residue field with a chosen coefficient-field section, and coordinate differentiation |
| `stalkOrder`, `stalkIdeal_affine`, `idealOrder_eq_iInf`, `idealOrder_span` | §1.2 | Localized ideal order, valued in ℕ∪{∞}, and its formal-chart and finite-generator comparisons over Noetherian local rings |
| `sncBoundary`, `sncBoundary_empty`, `sncBoundary_restrict`, `sncBoundary_coordinate` | §1.3 | Finite globally labelled smooth components, simultaneous coordinates and open restriction, retaining birth order when transforms are used |
| `markedIdeal`, `weightedPresentation_commonMark`, `markedIdeal_rescale` | §1.4 | Positive marks, weighted presentations and common-mark test equivalence on smooth ambient schemes |
| `permissibleCentre`, `permissibleCentre_idealPower`, `permissibleCentre_boundaryContained`, `permissibleCentre_snc_after` | §1.5 | Smooth closed centres in the cosupport, simultaneous SNC and the ideal-power condition for controlled division |
| `controlledTransform`, `controlledTransform_factor`, `controlledTransform_identityCartier`, `controlledTransform_flatBaseChange` | §1.6 | Image-ideal pullback divided by the marked exceptional power; the strict and weak transforms retain their separate meanings |
| `testEquivalence`, `presentationEquivalent_equivalence`, `presentationEquivalent_transform`, `presentationEquivalent_strength` | §1.7 | Blowup, product and exceptional test policies with their history, including the fixed old label in the restricted exceptional policy |
| `normalizedOrders`, `normalizedOrder_commonMark`, `exceptionalOrder_divisibility`, `residualOrder_nonnegative` | §1.8 | Point order, labelled generic boundary divisibility and residual order, with a separate infinite case |

Source: Bierstone–Milman 1997, §§3.1–3.8, pp. 231–234; Example 3.12, pp. 236–237;
§§4.1–4.10, pp. 241–244; Construction 4.23, p. 247; the precise export statements are
ResolutionOfSingularitiesCharacteristicZero §§1.1–1.9.

### 9.1a Order and marked sums

Consume ResolutionOfSingularitiesCharacteristicZero §1.10's affine order and marked-sum API in
its namespace `ResolutionOfSingularities`. Affine localization agrees with `stalkOrder` above.
Positive-mark rescaling and the marked-sum cosupport intersection use regular localizations;
closed cosupport uses finite type over a characteristic-zero field and regularity. There is one
affine marked-ideal carrier, with the supplier's positive mark, and one order function.
The sum of marks a,b has ideal `I^b + J^a` and mark `ab`.
(Source: Bierstone–Milman 1997, §§4.1–4.2 and Construction 4.23, pp. 241, 247.)

### 9.2a Derivative ideals

Consume ResolutionOfSingularitiesCharacteristicZero §2.15's polynomial derivative-ideal API.
It includes the original ideal and all first partial derivatives. Its finite-variable
characteristic-zero maximal-contact assertion gives an order-one element in the `(d−1)`-st
iterate at a prime of ideal order `d>0`. The boundary-transverse hypothesis of §9.2 remains
necessary when using such an equation as a contact presentation with boundary.
(Source: Bierstone–Milman 1997, Proposition 4.12 and Remarks 4.13, p. 244; pp. 251–252.)

### 9.4 Principalization and preservation of the resolved locus

Consume ResolutionOfSingularitiesCharacteristicZero §§5.1–5.5 and §7.8 through the following
comparisons on the common scheme and blowup carriers.

| Comparison names | Supplier export | Contract used here |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `principalization` | §5.1, `principalization` | For a coherent ideal generically nonzero on every component of a smooth finite-type characteristic-zero scheme, the total transform is an invertible monomial ideal with strict-SNC support; the weak transform is the unit ideal and the complement of the ideal's zero locus is unchanged |
| `embeddedResolution` | §5.2, `embeddedResolution` | For a reduced closed subscheme of a smooth finite-type characteristic-zero ambient scheme with empty initial boundary, a smooth strict transform simultaneous-SNC with the exceptional boundary, preserving the entire regular locus |
| `resolvedLocus`, `resolvedLocus_subsetCriterion`, `resolvedLocus_open`, `resolvedLocus_restrict` | §5.3, same names | Smooth embedded schemes with labelled SNC boundary not containing any component: the simultaneous-coordinate locus equals the smooth expected-codimension subset-intersection locus |
| `preserveResolvedPoints`, `smoothPairCleanup` | §5.4, `preserveResolvedPoints` (also `smoothPairCleanup`) | Smooth-pair cleanup with centres in the unresolved locus, retaining every initially resolved point |
| `localIsomorphismResolution` | §5.5, `localIsomorphismResolution`; §7.8, `resolution_field` | Every reduced finite-type characteristic-zero scheme has a projective birational smooth-source resolution preserving its entire regular locus; local-isomorphism comparison retains the resolving towers after empty steps are omitted |

For §9.10, `principalization` identifies the total ideal with `O(−F)` for its effective
SNC-supported divisor F; `localIsomorphismResolution` supplies the smooth birational source used
in `resolutionCanonicalDegreeBound`. These are applications of the supplier's field theorem,
including reducible schemes, with no integrality restriction on the supplied resolution contract.
(Source: Bierstone–Milman 1997, Theorem 1.10, pp. 216–217; Theorems 11.14, 12.2, 12.4 and 13.2,
pp. 290–298; ResolutionOfSingularitiesCharacteristicZero §§5.1–5.5, 7.8.)

**Checks.**

- For the unit ideal the supplied principalization has F=0, so the multiplier-ideal application in §9.10 gives `O_X`.
- An ideal zero on one component and unit on another has no invertible total transform on the zero component; it does not meet `principalization`'s generic-nonzero hypothesis.
- A smooth projective hypersurface of degree δ and dimension p uses the identity resolution, and the canonical-degree comparison of §9.10 is adjunction `ω_Y = O_Y(δ−p−2)`.

### 9.5 SNC compactification and Cartier separation

Consume ResolutionOfSingularitiesCharacteristicZero §6.2's `sncCompactification` for every smooth
quasi-projective finite-type scheme U over a characteristic-zero field. The comparison retains
the prescribed dense open U, a smooth projective compactification, and its reduced strict-SNC
boundary with globally smooth labelled components. The names `sncCompactification_open`,
`sncCompactification_boundary` and `sncCompactification_projective` identify these three supplier
comparisons. Projectivity is part of the export, including the chosen projective closure and its
projective modifications. The SNC boundary is the one used for `logDeRhamComplex` in §9.10.
(Source: Bierstone–Milman 1997, Theorems 1.10, 11.14, 12.2 and 13.2, pp. 216–217, 290–298;
ResolutionOfSingularitiesCharacteristicZero §§6.1–6.2.)

Consume ResolutionOfSingularitiesCharacteristicZero §6.3's `cartierSeparation` for two effective
Cartier divisors on any scheme X. On the blowup of the sum of their invertible ideals, write
`p*D_i = F + D′_i`; the residual divisors have disjoint support and
`p*D₁ + D′₂ = p*D₂ + D′₁`. The comparison names `cartierSeparation_residual`,
`cartierSeparation_disjoint` and `cartierSeparation_difference` retain these identities on the
same blowup. Cartier divisors here mean invertible ideal sheaves with regular local equations,
so this contract applies without smoothness, integrality, Noetherianity or characteristic
hypotheses. (Boxer–Pilloni, §4.1.10, Proposition-construction 4.1.11, p. 42;
ResolutionOfSingularitiesCharacteristicZero §6.3.)

**Checks.**

- For `U = 𝔾_m²` in `ℙ¹×ℙ¹`, the compactification comparison retains all four labelled boundary components in the logarithmic complex of §9.10.
- On `ℙ¹` with its single boundary point, the labelled local equation gives the same dlog generator as `LogCrystalline.logDifferentials`.
- If `D₁=2[0]` and `D₂=3[0]` on `𝔸¹`, the identity blowup of `(t²)` has F=`2[0]`, `D′₁=0`, `D′₂=[0]`; the comparison retains the residual multiplicity one.

### 9.7 Relative embedded resolution with an initial boundary

Consume ResolutionOfSingularitiesCharacteristicZero §5.6's `relativeEmbeddedResolution` for a
reduced closed finite-type subscheme X of a smooth separated ambient scheme over any
characteristic-zero field, with a finite ordered SNC boundary E no component of which contains a
component of X. The comparison gives the same finite permissible blowup tower, smooth strict
transform simultaneous-SNC with the transformed initial and exceptional boundary, and identity
over the original smooth simultaneous-SNC locus. With empty E this recovers preservation of the
entire regular locus in `embeddedResolution`; with nonempty E the isomorphism locus is the
resolved pair locus. This is the boundary comparison used together with §9.5's logarithmic carrier.
(Source: Bierstone–Milman 1997, tower (6.7), pp. 255–256; Theorems 12.2 and 12.4 and
Lemmas 12.5, 12.7–12.8, pp. 292–295; ResolutionOfSingularitiesCharacteristicZero §5.6.)

**Checks.**

- On `X:y=x²` in `𝔸²` with `E:x=0`, the differentials dy and dx at the origin are independent; the comparison preserves that point and its reduced restricted boundary.
- For the same X with `E:y=0`, the restricted boundary has ideal `(x²)`; cleanup can modify the origin, and the comparison does not identify this with the original reduced-boundary chart.
- If `X:x=0` and `E:x=0`, the restricted equation is identically zero; this pair is excluded from the boundary comparison and supplies no SNC chart for §9.10.

### 9.10 Algebraic vanishing and numerical inputs

The numerical very-ampleness theorem uses an algebraic route through the algebraic adjoint-vanishing and intersection bounds below. Use basic projective geometry from 1.1–1.5 and the resolution and principalization supplied by ResolutionOfSingularitiesCharacteristicZero through the comparisons in §§9.1–9.7. The vanishing inputs below and the bounds in 9.11 then follow in this order. All varieties in this paragraph are smooth, projective and geometrically integral over a characteristic-zero field unless stated otherwise. Numerical intersections and Serre duality are those of SchemeAndStackFoundations Layer 5 and §2.20; the surface Hodge-index theorem is SchemeAndStackFoundations §5.10's for the mixed-intersection inequality below.

Call a reduced divisor `D=ΣD_i` on a smooth k-scheme X SNC relative to k if, étale locally on X, there is an étale map `X→𝔸ⁿ_k` with coordinates `x_1,…,x_n` such that D is `V(x_1⋯x_r)` and each component through the point is one `V(x_i)`; equivalently each scheme-theoretic intersection `D_J` of |J| components is smooth over k of codimension |J|. Over a perfect field this is the absolute SNC condition of SchemeAndStackFoundations §4.17, since a regular finite-type scheme over a perfect field is smooth. If k is a regular Noetherian ring and X is of finite type over k, relative SNC implies that X is a regular Noetherian scheme and that D is absolutely SNC: X is regular because it is smooth over a regular ring, and at a point x of `D_J` the quotient `O_(X,x)/(x_i : i∈J)` is the local ring of `D_J`, regular of dimension `dim O_(X,x)−|J|`, so the images of these `x_i` in `m_x/m_x²` are independent and extend to a regular system of parameters (Stacks, Lemmas 10.163.10 and 10.106.3, tags 07NF and 00NQ; Definition 41.21.1, tag 0BI9). Over such a base the converse fails (the check `LogDeRhamChecks.absoluteOnly`), and over a singular base relative SNC need not be absolute SNC, nor X regular (the check `LogDeRhamChecks.singularBase`). Define `logDeRhamComplex X D`, for a scheme X smooth and of finite type over a regular Noetherian ring k and a reduced divisor D SNC relative to k, as CrystallineCohomology §CR.5.1's `LogCrystalline.logDeRham` for the divisorial log structure `LogCrystalline.divisorialLog D` of §CR.5:log-algebra.4 over the trivial log structure on `Spec k`; no second complex is constructed. The regular Noetherian base is what places `(X,D)` inside the regular Noetherian absolute-SNC scope of that constructor, by the implication above. By the presentation of CrystallineCohomology §CR.5.1 (`LogCrystalline.logDifferentials`) computed on such a relative chart, its degree-one module is free on `dx_i/x_i` for boundary coordinates and `dx_j` for the others, and degree a is its exterior power; in particular every `Ω^a_X(log D)` is locally free of finite rank. The absolute SNC condition alone does not give this: the divisorial log structure exists, but its log differentials can have torsion along D. The differential extends the universal log derivation by the graded Leibniz rule and is k-linear, not `O_X`-linear: `d(f·ω)`=df∧`ω+f·dω`. Changes of SNC coordinates identify these modules and differentials, so this is a complex of k-modules on the small étale site, not a complex depending on one selected chart. Its API `logDeRhamComplex.degree`, `logDeRhamComplex.d`, `logDeRhamComplex.d_sq`, `logDeRhamComplex.etalePullback`, `logDeRhamComplex.residue` gives these modules, the differential, `d²=0` (from the log de Rham differential of CrystallineCohomology §CR.5.1), étale comparison and, added here, the residue along a labelled component. Our residue puts the labelled dlog factor first: `res_x(dlog x∧α)=α`. The last-factor ordering in Esnault–Viehweg is related by the exterior sign `(−1)^(a−1)` in degree a; the two conventions are transported with this sign. For disjoint labelled reduced divisors A,B whose union is SNC relative to k, the compact-boundary complex `logDeRhamComplex.withCompactBoundary A B` is the subcomplex `I_B·Ω•_X(log(A+B))` of `Ω•_X(log(A+B))`, where `I_B` is the ideal of B. It is stable under d because `d(fω)=f`·(dlog `f∧ω+dω`) for a local equation f of B, and dlog f is a section of `Ω¹_X`(log(`A+B`)). By `logDeRhamComplex.compactBoundaryTensor` below its graded module is `Ω•(log(A+B))⊗O(−B)`, and the compact-boundary API is stated through that identification; its differential is the restriction of d, not d tensored with an `O_X`-linear map. In Esnault–Viehweg's notation `Ω•(A,B)=Ω•(log(A+B))(−A)` the twisted divisor is the first label, so this complex is their Ω•`(B,A)`. (CrystallineCohomology §CR.5:log-algebra.4 (`LogCrystalline.divisorialLog`) and §CR.5.1 (`LogCrystalline.logDifferentials`, `LogCrystalline.logDeRham`); Esnault–Viehweg, §2, Definition 2.1, Properties 2.2–2.3, pp. 11–13; Notation 9.16, p. 103; §10, Definitions 10.14 and Theorem 10.16, pp. 114–116.)

**Checks.**

- `LogDeRhamChecks.empty`: in dimension zero with empty boundary, the complex is O in degree zero and zero in positive degrees; all residues vanish.
- `LogDeRhamChecks.one`: on the affine line with boundary `x=0`, `d(x^m)=m x^m dx/x`. In characteristic p, `d(x^p)=0`, although `x^p` is nonzero.
- `LogDeRhamChecks.two`: on the crossing xy=0, the ordered two-form is `dx/x∧dy/y`; swapping the labels negates it, and residue along x sends this form to `dy/y` with this order convention.
- `LogDeRhamChecks.compact`: when B is `x=0` on the line, the compact-boundary complex includes `O(−B)→Ω¹(log B)⊗O(−B)`; it is not the untwisted logarithmic complex.
- `LogDeRhamChecks.scalarLinear`: on the affine line, `d(x·1)`=dx whereas `x·d(1)=0`, so the differential is linear over the base and not over `O_X`; in the compact-boundary complex `d(x)=x`·dlog x lies in `I_B·Ω¹`(log B).
- `LogDeRhamChecks.absoluteOnly`: for `k=ℚ[t]`, `X=Spec k` over itself and `D=V(t)`, D is SNC on the regular scheme X but not relative to k (it is not smooth over k of codimension one). The divisorial log differentials are `k·dlog t/(t·dlog t)≅k/(t)`, since `dt=0` relative to k; so `I_D·Ω¹`(log D)`=0` while `Ω¹`(log D)`⊗O(−D)≅k/(t)≠0`. This pair is excluded from `logDeRhamComplex`.
- `LogDeRhamChecks.singularBase`: for the cuspidal base `k=ℚ[u,v]/(v²−u³)`, `X=𝔸¹_k=Spec k[x]` and `D=V(x)≅Spec k`, the identity chart makes D SNC relative to k, yet the local ring of X at `(u,v,x)` has dimension 2 and embedding dimension 3, so X is not regular and D is not absolutely SNC there. This pair lies outside the divisorial log constructor and is excluded from `logDeRhamComplex` by the regular Noetherian base hypothesis.

Prove `logDeRhamComplex.compactBoundaryTensor`. Let X be smooth and of finite type over a regular Noetherian ring k and A,B disjoint labelled reduced divisors with `A+B` SNC relative to k. Then each `Ω^a_X(log(A+B))` is locally free of finite rank, and multiplication `Ω^a_X(log(A+B))⊗O_X(−B)→I_B·Ω^a_X(log(A+B))` is an isomorphism of `O_X`-modules for every a, compatible with étale pullback. Hence `logDeRhamComplex.withCompactBoundary A B` has graded module `Ω•(log(A+B))⊗O(−B)`.

Here k is a regular Noetherian ring (fields, ℤ, Dedekind rings and their polynomial rings are allowed) and X is of finite type over k, so that `(X,A+B)` lies in the scope of the divisorial log constructor; the relative SNC chart is essential, and the absolute SNC condition does not suffice.

(Esnault–Viehweg, §2, Properties 2.2(b)–(c), pp. 11–12, over a field; Stacks, de Rham Cohomology, Definition 50.15.1 (tag 0FMV) and Lemma 50.15.2 (tag 0FMW), which impose the corresponding torsion-freeness of relative differentials.)

For the proof, work étale locally on a relative chart, where the boundary coordinates `x_i` are local equations of the components and `LogCrystalline.divisorialLog.boundary_chart` gives the chart `ℕ^r→O_X` they define: the log differentials are free on the displayed basis by the presentation of CrystallineCohomology §CR.5.1 and étale invariance of Kähler differentials, so their exterior powers are free; tensoring a locally free module with the invertible ideal `I_B` is injective into it, with image `I_B·Ω^a`. The identifications glue because changes of relative chart act by invertible matrices.

*Needs:* `logDeRhamComplex`, CrystallineCohomology §CR.5:log-algebra.4 (`LogCrystalline.divisorialLog.boundary_chart`) and §CR.5.1 (`LogCrystalline.logDifferentials`).

**Checks.**

- `CompactTensorChecks.line`: on `𝔸¹_k` with `B=V(x)` and `A=∅`, `Ω¹`(log B) is free on dlog x and `I_B·Ω¹`(log B) is free on `x·dlog x=dx`, matching `O(−B)·dlog x`.
- `CompactTensorChecks.emptyB`: for `B=∅` the ideal is `O_X` and the map is the identity of `Ω•_X(log A)`.
- `CompactTensorChecks.absoluteOnly`: for the pair of `LogDeRhamChecks.absoluteOnly`, the multiplication map in degree one is `k/(t)→0`, not injective; the relative SNC hypothesis cannot be dropped.
- `CompactTensorChecks.singularBase`: the pair of `LogDeRhamChecks.singularBase` (cuspidal k, `X=𝔸¹_k`, `B=V(x)`) is relatively SNC but X is not regular, so the theorem makes no assertion about it; the regular base hypothesis is not implied by relative SNC.

Prove `logFrobeniusSplitting`: over a perfect field of characteristic `p>0`, if the smooth pair `(X,D)` lifts to `W₂` and `i<p`, there is an isomorphism in the derived category from `⊕_{a≤i} Ω^a_(X^(p))(log D^(p))[−a]` to `τ≤i F_*Ω•_X(log D)`. In particular the full complex splits when `dim X<p`. The degree-one local splitting is division by p of the differential of a lifted Frobenius. Differences on double overlaps are derivations, providing the Čech homotopy; its triple equation gives descent of the chain map. Exterior powers and antisymmetrization divide by a!, which is invertible for `a<p`. Cartier's local coordinate computation proves that the map induces the required cohomology isomorphism. The `W₂` lift and this strict degree bound are essential. (Esnault–Viehweg, §9, Theorem 9.14, and §10, Theorem 10.16 and proof, pp. 114–116.)

Prove `compactBoundaryFrobeniusComparison`. Over a perfect field k of characteristic `p>0`, let X be smooth over k, `D=A+B` with A,B disjoint labelled reduced divisors and D SNC (relative to k, which over the perfect field k is the absolute condition), `F:X→X′` the relative Frobenius, and `B′`,`D′` the base changes to `X′`. Then: `(a)` the projection formula and `F^*O_(X′)(−B′)=O_X`(−pB) give an isomorphism of complexes of `O_(X′)`-modules `F_*Ω•_X(log D)⊗O_(X′)(−B′)≅F_*(I_B^p·Ω•_X(log D))`; `(b)` the inclusion `F_*`(`I_B^p·Ω•_X(log D)`)→`F_*`(`logDeRhamComplex.withCompactBoundary A B`) is a quasi-isomorphism; `(c)` the Cartier isomorphism of `logFrobeniusSplitting`, twisted by `O_(X′)(−B′)`, gives `Ω^a_(X′)`(log `D′`)⊗`O_(X′)(−B′)≅H^a`(`F_*`(`logDeRhamComplex.withCompactBoundary A B`)). These identifications commute with étale pullback. The two complexes in `(b)` are not equal; their quotient is acyclic.

Here k perfect of characteristic `p>0`; X smooth over k; A,B disjoint with `A+B` SNC; B is the twisted label.

(Esnault–Viehweg, Lemma 2.7, p. 15, and Lemma 2.10 with proof, pp. 16–17; Notation 9.16 and Corollary 9.17 with proof, p. 103, where the twisted label is the first one.)

For the proof, `(a)` is the projection formula for the finite flat morphism F. For `(b)`, factor the inclusion through the subcomplexes `I_B^(j+1)·Ω`•⊂`I_B^j·Ω`• for `1≤j≤p−1`; the connection d on `O_X`(−jB) has residue j along every component of B, which is a unit in k for these j, so each inclusion is a quasi-isomorphism by the residue criterion; locally the quotients are the acyclic complexes of the first check. For `(c)`, combine `(a)`, `(b)` and the Cartier isomorphism for `Ω•_X(log D)`.

*Needs:* `logDeRhamComplex`, `logDeRhamComplex.compactBoundaryTensor`, `logFrobeniusSplitting`, SchemeAndStackFoundations Layer 2.

**Checks.**

- `CompactFrobeniusChecks.line`: on `A¹` with `B=(x)` and `A=∅`, the quotient `I_B·Ω`•/`I_B^p·Ω`• has basis `x^j` in degree 0 and `x^j`·dlog x in degree 1 for `1≤j≤p−1`, with `d(x^j)=j·x^j`·dlog x; each j is a unit mod p, so the quotient is acyclic.
- `CompactFrobeniusChecks.notEqual`: for `p=2` on the same line, the two complexes differ in degree 0 by the class of x, so `(b)` is a quasi-isomorphism and not an equality; tensoring `F_*Ω`•(log B) with `O_(X′)(−B′)` twists by 2B, not by B.
- `CompactFrobeniusChecks.emptyB`: for `B=∅` both complexes are `Ω•_X(log A)` and the comparison is the identity.

Prove `compactBoundaryFrobeniusSplitting`. In the situation of `logFrobeniusSplitting`, with `D=A+B` and a W₂(k)-lift of `(X,D)`, for `i<p` the lifted splitting induces an isomorphism in the derived category from `⊕_(a≤i) Ω^a_(X′)`(log `D′`)⊗`O_(X′)(−B′)[−a]` to `τ≤i F_*`(`logDeRhamComplex.withCompactBoundary A B`). For `dim X<p` this splits the whole compact-boundary complex.

Here the hypotheses of `logFrobeniusSplitting`; A,B disjoint with `A+B` SNC; the `W₂` lift is of the pair `(X,D)`.

(Esnault–Viehweg, Corollary 10.17 and proof, pp. 116–117, with the labels exchanged because their Ω•`(A,B)` twists the first label.)

For the proof, twist the splitting of `τ≤i F_*Ω•_X(log D)` given by `logFrobeniusSplitting` by the invertible `O_(X′)(−B′)`, identify the target with `τ≤i F_*(I_B^p·Ω•_X(log D))` by `compactBoundaryFrobeniusComparison``(a)`, and compose with the quasi-isomorphism `(b)`; the composite induces the twisted Cartier isomorphism `(c)` on cohomology, so it is an isomorphism in the derived category.

*Needs:* `logFrobeniusSplitting`, `compactBoundaryFrobeniusComparison`.

**Checks.**

- `CompactSplittingChecks.emptyB`: `B=∅` recovers `logFrobeniusSplitting` for the pair `(X,A)`.
- `CompactSplittingChecks.projectiveLine`: on `P¹` with B a point and `A=∅`, the graded pieces are `O(−1)` in degree 0 and `Ω¹` in degree 1; the only nonzero Hodge group is `H¹(Ω¹)`, of dimension one, matching the one-dimensional hypercohomology.
- `CompactSplittingChecks.labels`: on `P¹` with a point as A and `B=∅` the only nonzero Hodge group is `H⁰(O)`, in bidegree (0,0), whereas with the same point as B it is `H¹(Ω¹)`, in bidegree (1,1); the label carrying the twist is material.

Prove `logHodgeDegeneration`: for a smooth proper characteristic-zero scheme and SNC `D=A+B`, the spectral sequence with `E₁^{a,b}=H^b(X,Ω^a(log D)⊗O(−B))`, the hypercohomology spectral sequence of `logDeRhamComplex.withCompactBoundary A B`, degenerates at `E₁`. Spread the pair to a smooth proper model over a finite-type Z-algebra with boundary SNC relative to that base, and shrink the base to a regular affine open (the regular locus of a reduced finite-type ℤ-algebra is open and dense), so that `logDeRhamComplex.compactBoundaryTensor` applies on the model; shrink so the finitely many coherent and hypercohomology modules used are locally free with base change. At a good closed point with `p>dim X` the compact-boundary splitting `compactBoundaryFrobeniusSplitting` makes the sum of Hodge dimensions equal the hypercohomology dimension. Equality of these ranks on the model gives degeneration at the characteristic-zero generic fibre. Smooth models provide the `W₂` lift after choosing a suitable unramified lift of that closed point. This argument uses proper coherent base change, the finite complex and local Cartier calculation, and no analytic comparison. (Esnault–Viehweg, Corollary 10.23 and proof, p. 124; the relative version is Theorem 10.21, pp. 121–123.)
*Needs:* `compactBoundaryFrobeniusSplitting`, `logDeRhamComplex`, `logDeRhamComplex.compactBoundaryTensor`, StableReduction Layer 2, SchemeAndStackFoundations §0.9.

Prove `cyclicCoverEigensummand`: for an invertible L, a nonzero section of `L^N` with SNC divisor `D=Σα_jD_j`, and N prime to the characteristic, the normalized root cover has eigensummand `L^(−i)⊗O(⌊iD/N⌋)` for `0≤i<N`. Its logarithmic connection has residue equal to the fractional part of `iα_j/N` in the field; integral residues remove the corresponding boundary component. Root-cover coordinate charts prove this formula, and normalizing the monomials proves the floor, including its sign. The local quotient singularities are resolved using Layer 9; trace splits the finite cover because N is invertible. Apply logarithmic degeneration to the resolved cover and its character summands. Consequently, for `0<α_j<N` in characteristic zero, every effective divisor B supported on D gives a surjection `H^q(L^(−1)(−B))→H^q(L^(−1))`. Enlarging to an SNC divisor and using the version with compact boundary gives the corresponding restriction maps with extra labelled components. (Esnault–Viehweg, Theorem 3.2, pp. 19–21; §§3.6–3.11, pp. 22–25; Theorem 5.1, pp. 42–43.)

Prove `algebraicAdjointVanishing`: if a rational divisor A on a smooth projective characteristic-zero variety is nef and big, with fractional support SNC, then `H^q(X,ω_X⊗O(⌈A⌉))=0` for `q>0`. The integral ample case is Kodaira vanishing; the nef-and-big case is Kawamata–Viehweg vanishing. Clear denominators, write a sufficiently large multiple as an ample divisor plus an effective divisor, resolve their union, apply the cyclic-cover restriction surjection, and kill the source by Serre vanishing and duality. The round-up comes from the dual of the floor in the root-cover summand. The birational comparison retains the higher-direct-image vanishing; a finite quotient chart is reduced to a smooth cover by trace, and the Leray induction proves rationality of that quotient. (Esnault–Viehweg, Corollaries 5.2 and 5.6, pp. 43–46; Corollary 5.12`(c)` and Claim 5.13 with proofs, pp. 48–52.) No unrestricted positive-characteristic vanishing is used: the source's positive-characteristic variant requires a W₂ lift, dimension bound and a root exponent prime to p.

Define `algebraicMultiplierIdeal` for a nonzero coherent ideal a on a smooth characteristic-zero variety and a nonnegative rational c. On a principalization `π:Y→X`, write `a O_Y=O_Y(−F)` and set `J(a^c)=π_*O_Y(K_(Y/X)−⌊cF⌋)`. Define it as an ideal in `O_X` through the canonical rational-function identification. Common domination, the local root-cover vanishing and the projection formula prove independence of π and vanishing of the positive direct images in this formula. Its API `algebraicMultiplierIdeal.ofPrincipal`, `algebraicMultiplierIdeal.ofUnit`, `algebraicMultiplierIdeal.monotone`, `algebraicMultiplierIdeal.resolutionIndependent`, `algebraicMultiplierIdeal.localVanishing` records the principal SNC formula, the unit ideal, reverse inclusion as c grows, independence and vanishing. If `a⊗M` is globally generated and `L−cM` is nef and big, the same calculation on Y gives `H^q(X,ω_X⊗L⊗J(a^c))=0` for `q>0`. This is the algebraic case of the multiplier-ideal vanishing used in the effective argument. (Demailly, §1, Theorem 1.2 and formula (1.4), pp. 3–5, and the algebraic-use statement at the start of §2, p. 5; the algebraic proof is the preceding root-cover and birational vanishing.)

**Checks.**

- `MultiplierIdealChecks.unit`: the unit ideal has `F=0` and multiplier ideal `O_X` for every c; no support is introduced.
- `MultiplierIdealChecks.principal`: for the ideal `(x²)` of the line and `c=1/2` the multiplier ideal is `(x)`; for `c=1/3` it is O. The floor is applied after multiplication by 2.
- `MultiplierIdealChecks.crossing`: for `(xy)` on the plane and `c=1`, the multiplier ideal is `(xy)`; both boundary components are retained.
- `MultiplierIdealChecks.nonExample`: the zero ideal has no finite divisor F on a principalization and is excluded from this definition; it cannot be assigned the unit-ideal formula.

Prove `uniformAdjointVeryAmpleness`: `K_X+(n+1)L` is nef for ample L, and there is a positive integer `λ_n` depending only on n such that `m(K_X+(n+2)L)+G` is very ample for every `m≥λ_n` and nef G. One may take `λ_n=max(1, binom(3n+1,n)−2n)` for `n≥1`. For the proof, apply multiplier-ideal vanishing to ideals of algebraic sections, choose sections outside each positive-dimensional multiplier support by the numerical-polynomial root bound, and strictly enlarge its coherent ideal. Noetherianity leaves only a finite support. Jet restrictions then surject by `H¹` vanishing. The descending integer recurrence `b_(k+1)=floor(a(b_k+η)/(a+1))+1` stops at `a(η+1)+1`; with no imposed jets `η=n`, taking `a→∞` proves nefness of `K+(n+1)L`. With two point jets or one first-order jet, take `a=1` and the binomial jet-length bound. This yields the adjoint very-ampleness constant and its stability under nef addition. This proof uses only the algebraic multiplier ideals just constructed, HRR and coherent exact sequences, although the source writes the same ideals using weights of sections. (Demailly, Theorems 2.3 and 2.4 with proofs, pp. 6–10, and Theorem 0.2`(c)`, p. 2.)

Prove `nefMixedIntersectionBound`: for ample L, nef H and `v=L^n>0`, `H^p L^(n−p)≤(H L^(n−1))^p/v^(p−1)` for `1≤p≤n`. Cut to surfaces by general ample divisors, apply the supplied surface Hodge-index theorem, and use induction for the log-concavity of mixed intersections; take a limit after adding positive rational ample classes to nef factors. The dimensions zero and one need no surface cutting. This is the specific higher-dimensional inequality needed below, not a new copy of the supplied surface theorem.

Prove `resolutionCanonicalDegreeBound`: for an integral p-dimensional subvariety Y in a very ample embedding H of degree δ, its Grauert–Riemenschneider canonical sheaf `ω_Y^GR=ρ_*ω_(Ỹ)` has a nonzero map to `O_Y((δ−p−2)H)`. A general projection is finite and birational to a hypersurface of degree δ. The canonical trace embeds the resolution canonical sheaf in the hypersurface's dualizing line; its rational-form identification and pullback into `O_Y` give the asserted map. This uses the resolution canonical sheaf, which need not equal the dualizing sheaf of a non-rational singularity. On a smooth hypersurface the bound is an equality. Combining adjoint vanishing on the resolution, HRR, and the fact that a degree-p nonzero polynomial has at most p integer roots gives a nonzero section of `ω_Y^GR⊗O_Y(mL−B)` for some `m≤p(B L^(p−1)Y)/(L^pY)+p+1`, when L is ample and B nef. (Demailly, Theorem 3.1 and its projection proof, pp. 11–12; Proposition 4.6, p. 13.)

These inputs prove `numericalVeryAmpleness` as follows. Set `H=λ_n(K+(n+2)L)` and `h=H L^(n−1)=λ_n(w+(n+2)v)`. For `n≥2`, the descending-cycle proof of Demailly's Theorem 4.7 gives a bound depending only on n,v,h and `b=B L^(n−1)`: start with a bounded section of `m_n L−B`, then on each integral p-dimensional component use the preceding canonical-degree and adjoint-section estimates to choose bounded `m_p`. Intersections bound the next component degrees by products of the already chosen `m_j` and `h^p/v^(p−1)`. Finite products and the recurrence in that proof therefore give one numerical bound; no individual Hilbert-polynomial coefficient occurs. For a curve not contained in the last one-dimensional stratum, the first section that does not vanish identically on it proves nonnegative degree of `m_0L−B`; for a curve in that stratum, its bounded degree and the positive integral degree of L give the same conclusion after increasing `m_0`. Thus `m_0L−B` is nef. Replace B by `B+H` and add H to get a very ample `mL−B` for every sufficiently large m. With `B=0` this gives the required uniform exponent. The displayed h is positive because H is ample. For `n=1`, the degree criterion gives very ampleness whenever `mv≥w+3`; the degree-one projective line is included. For `n=0` the geometric integral variety is a point and exponent 1 suffices. The complete embedding satisfies `h⁰(L^m)≤m^n v+n`, by the nondegenerate degree bound in projective space. (Demailly, Lemma 4.1, Proposition 4.3 and Corollary 4.4, pp. 12–13; Theorem 4.7 and proof, pp. 14–16.)

### 9.11 Uniform numerical boundedness

Prove `numericalVeryAmpleness`. For each dimension `d≥1` and integers `v>0`,w, there is `m₀(d,v,w)` such that for every smooth projective complex d-fold X and ample L with `L^d=v` and `K_X·L^(d−1)=w`, every `L^m` with `m≥m₀` is very ample. There are bounds for `h⁰(X,L^m₀)` depending only on these numerical data. The result includes the `K_X` trivial case `w=0` used by Charles; it is a uniform numerical assertion, not Serre’s bound for one fixed X.

Here `d≥1`; X a smooth projective complex variety (geometrically integral), ample L, fixed dimension and the two displayed intersection numbers. Intersection products and the canonical bundle are those of SchemeAndStackFoundations Layer 5 and §2.20.

([Demailly](https://www-fourier.univ-grenoble-alpes.fr/~demailly/manuscripts/very_ample.pdf), Theorems 2.3 and 2.4, pp. 6–10; Theorem 4.7 and proof, pp. 14–16; [Esnault–Viehweg](https://page.mi.fu-berlin.de/esnault/books/esvibuch.pdf), Corollary 5.12(c), pp. 48–52; Theorem 10.16, pp. 114–116; Corollary 10.23, p. 124).

For the proof, use the algebraic vanishing and effective adjoint chain of §9.10: logarithmic Frobenius splitting and characteristic-zero degeneration give cyclic-cover vanishing; principalization gives the algebraic multiplier ideals; HRR and the ideal-enlargement recurrence give uniform adjoint very ampleness. The descending-cycle and mixed-intersection argument then gives an exponent depending only on dimension, `L^d` and `K_X L^(d−1)`; then separate the curve case using degree `m deg L≥deg K_X+3` and the dimension-zero point. Once `L^m` is very ample, the nondegenerate complete embedding has `h⁰≤m^d v+d`. ResolutionOfSingularitiesCharacteristicZero supplies the resolution input independently of this vanishing chain, as stated in §9.10.

*Needs:* `amplePowersAndFixedTwists`, `hilbertPolynomial`, `uniformQuotientRegularity`, SchemeAndStackFoundations Layer 5, SchemeAndStackFoundations §5.3, SchemeAndStackFoundations Layer 4.

Prove `smoothPolarizedBoundedness`. Fix `n≥1` and `r>0`. Smooth projective complex varieties X of dimension 2n with `K_X` trivial and an ample L satisfying `L^(2n)=r` form a bounded family of underlying varieties. A uniform power `L^m` embeds them into one fixed `P^N` with degree `m^(2n)r`. The bounded-support families of `boundedSupportParameters`, through the bounded-degree target, then supply finitely many finite-type projective parameter families, and finitely many Hilbert polynomials. These families need no Hilbert-functor representability; Layer 2 uses this polynomial finiteness in applications of the Hilbert schemes supplied by SchemeAndStackFoundations §4.14's `hilbert_quot_schemes`.

Here Ample L, not merely big; `K_X` trivial; fixed dimension and top self-intersection. This is a complex geometric family statement, not descent of L over a smaller field.

([François Charles](https://annals.math.princeton.edu/wp-content/uploads/annals-v184-n2-p04-p.pdf), §3, Lemma 3.5 and proof, pp.507–508).

For the proof, apply the numerical theorem with `w=0` to get a uniform very ample exponent and section-dimension bound. Increase the ambient dimension to one N by padding the section basis. The degree becomes `m^(2n)r`; then apply the reduced bounded-degree target, including its finite bounded-support-family construction, to the fixed `P^N` and degree bound. Its generic reduction, spreading and Noetherian induction produce the finite-type projective families of underlying reduced varieties. No Layer 2 result is used.

*Needs:* `numericalVeryAmpleness`, `boundedDegreeHilbertPolynomials`, `hilbertPolynomial`.

### Examples

The unit ideal gives a zero principalization divisor in the multiplier-ideal application. A smooth
hypersurface uses adjunction in the canonical-degree bound, and the four torus boundary components
remain distinct in the logarithmic complex.

### Dependencies

ResolutionOfSingularitiesCharacteristicZero Layers 1–6 and §7.8 supplies the resolution, marked-ideal,
resolved-pair and SNC interfaces of §§9.1–9.7. Layer 1 supplies the projective geometry used in the
applications. CrystallineCohomology §CR.5:log-algebra.4 (`LogCrystalline.divisorialLog`) and §CR.5.1
(`LogCrystalline.logDifferentials`, `LogCrystalline.logDeRham`) supply the carrier of §9.10 on that
SNC geometry, for pairs relatively SNC over a regular Noetherian base, which are absolutely SNC on a
regular Noetherian scheme as that constructor requires. Algebraic adjoint vanishing, multiplier ideals and uniform numerical boundedness are
constructed here using SchemeAndStackFoundations §§2.19–2.21 (duality) and Layer 5 (intersection
theory).

## Downstream consumers

ModularCurvesPartII uses rigidification (§5.1), finite correspondence descent (§5.3), closures
and normalization (§5.4), `picard_infinitesimal_lifting` (§7.3),
`arithmetic_normalization_genericallyEtale` (§7.5) and
`completedAtlasPresentation_equivalence` (§8.3). AbelianSchemesAndArithmeticModuli uses the Picard sheaves
and section rigidifications of §7.6.1, framed deformations, polarized boundedness,
`rigidLevelStructure` for its abelian level instances, and the finite-source restriction exports
of Layer 3 under their names here:
`ModuliDescent.weilRestriction`, `ModuliDescent.weilRestriction_baseChange`,
`ModuliDescent.weilRestriction_algebraicity`, `ModuliDescent.relativeHom_algebraicity` and
`ModuliDescent.finiteQuotientComparison`. PELModuli and ShimuraVarieties use the representability
theorems. ComplexComparisonPartII uses
`spaceDQCoh` and `spacePerfect` (§7.7) for its quasi-coherator and derived-limit constructions,
the independent representability inputs and Picard carriers of §7.3, the framed comparisons
of §8.3 and coherent dévissage (§2.3). ResolutionOfSingularitiesCharacteristicZero supplies the
shared algebraic resolution and SNC compactification interfaces; §§9.4–9.7 retain the named
consumption comparisons `localIsomorphismResolution`, `sncCompactification` and
`relativeEmbeddedResolution`. The algebraic vanishing and numerical boundedness applications
of §§9.10–9.11 remain exports of this roadmap.
